Knowledge for harmony
Harmony between dog and human is the most important condition for a trusting and learning relationship.
Before each training session, pause for a short while and calmly think through the next steps and possible alternatives.
Move forward reassured and radiate calm.
Your dog senses how you feel and will behave accordingly.
Harmony needs timelessness. Do not train under time pressure.
Harmony is the state in which the dog and you are, as far as possible, independent of distraction and the dog is oriented towards you.
Harmony can be trained. Sit together with your dog regularly, for at least 15 minutes, in a quiet place in nature.
Speak calmly to your dog.
Make calm and clear movements when you train with your dog.
Meet even difficult situations with calm and deliberation.
Be reliable towards your dog so that it can depend on you.
Be a role model for your dog through your behaviour. The way you are is the way your dog is.
Reflect on actions and situations, and only then continue with the next step once calm has returned.
Control your breathing and walking speed. Be calm and composed.
Recognise the basic harmonious state and maintain it as often as possible.
Recognising the basic harmonious state
A dog in the basic harmonious state shows a loose body posture and a soft facial expression with relaxed eyes and a closed or slightly open mouth.
The tail is carried in its breed-typical resting position. Breathing is calm and even.
The dog is responsive, orients itself towards you and shows interest in the surroundings and in activities.
It can lie down and rest even when something is happening in the surroundings.
Once your dog and you know this state, you recognise deviations earlier: changed body tension, panting without reason, fixating or loss of responsiveness.

Exercise: before each training session, check three points. How am I breathing? What is my body tension? Is my dog showing the basic harmonious state? Begin the training only when all three questions can be answered positively.
Breathing and pace as a tool
Slow, deep breathing with a prolonged exhalation demonstrably calms the human body. Heart rate and muscle tension decrease.
You can use this effect deliberately before you approach your dog or begin an exercise.
Your dog recognises your tension from your posture, movement pace and voice. Calm breathing changes all three.
Walk at an even, calm pace and avoid flaring, hectic and stressed reactions.
Calm and recovery as part of training
Dogs have a high need for rest. Adult dogs sleep and rest on average 12 to 14 hours a day, puppies and young dogs considerably more.
Too many stimuli and too little recovery make a dog more easily aroused and impair its ability to learn.
Plan a rest period after every training session and after every walk with many impressions.
Short training sessions with breaks are more effective than one long session without interruption.
A dog that lies down calmly and relaxes in your presence shows trust. Actively encourage this state and reward it.
Predictability gives security
Animals experience situations as less stressful when they can foresee and influence them.
Consistent routines before training, for example always the same greeting and the same announcement signal, show your dog what will happen next.
Reliable rules work in the same way: what is allowed today also applies tomorrow. This corresponds to your demand for reliability.
Announce changes gradually, for example a new place or a new exercise, and start there with simple requirements.

Note: all information on rest times is based on experience. Age, breed, state of health and daily routine influence the individual need. If your dog shows persistent restlessness or exhaustion despite sufficient rest, it may need to be checked by a vet.
Factors to avoid
By all means avoid misusing the dog as an outlet for stress and time pressure.
Avoid training with the dog when you are stressed or agitated.
Avoid going into training sessions unprepared.
Avoid training with the dog under time pressure or with set distances to cover.
In surprising situations, by all means avoid hectic behaviour, indecision and overreactions.
Avoid letting external circumstances influence you so much that you transfer stress to the dog.
Avoid processes that are too fast and training without pauses.
Avoid demanding results in difficult situations that have not yet been trained in easy ones.
Avoid being only in motion with the dog. Harmony needs periods of rest.
By all means avoid excited, hectic speech and speaking in a commanding tone.
Avoid breaking rules yourself. Either there is a rule or there is none.
Avoid feelings of frustration and disapproval towards the dog; they only unsettle it.
Practice impulse: the harmony anchor

Find a place in nature today and simply sit down with your dog for 15 minutes. Without a phone, without commands, without expectation. Breathe consciously and calmly, and observe how your dog's body tension adapts to your inner stillness.
Harmony is the peaceful basic state within a system.
Recognising the basic harmonious state is an essential tool.
Every disturbance of the basic harmonious state affects the dog's response patterns.
Harmony is a state. It is not a matter of the thinker.
Creating harmony must be a basic need.
Be harmonious with your dog.
